5ac62703424d: A family of marsh, dune and sea — and the story of a name that travelled on from the dunes.
df2dc57085a9: Between the North Sea and Nissum Fjord lies a stretch of land the wind has never quite let go of. The dunes wander. Sand settles along the field boundaries. Behind the line of dunes the ground sinks into low, wet stretches where the water does not run but seeps.
3cec64f1bcf9: A place like that was called a <t1>kær</t1> — a marsh.
c43d7eb72bdb: And one of them was called Silkjær.
b3ca3c70a060: Later the name was carried by fishermen, beach bailiffs, lifeboatmen, skippers and families who left the place but took it with them.
b70f2946c27b: The family’s history holds two shipwrecks, a religious revival, a prison sentence, secret voyages during the Occupation — and three sisters who, within six years, each gave a son the name Niels Silkjær.
dcbedae1be95: This is the story of the place, and of the people who made it a family name.
fa3181336184: The same first names return in every generation — there are eight Nielses and three Ane Johannes in what follows. If the threads become hard to hold, they are set out in the <t1>key to the names</t1> at the back, together with the <t2>family tree</t2>.
e9c848cf471c: Where the sources fall short, the text says so. The small circle<t1>?</t1> opens the caveat for what stands just before it: what is documented, what is inferred, and what is still a guess. All sources are gathered in the <t2>list of sources</t2>.
b2b8e56ec235: The chronicle sees the family from one particular place in the tree: the author’s. The six links below are the backbone of the work — it is from the last of them that the questions have been asked backwards, and that is why these very people, their brothers and sisters and their children, fill the chapters.
6f74293557da: The story does not always run straight. It follows first the smallholding and the beginning of the name, then several of Niels Thomsen’s ten children — the fishing skipper in Esbjerg, the gravedigger on Djursland — but each time it returns to the line here. And notice the quiet paradox: this very line lost the name along the way, when Ane Johanne married a Madsen and Laura a Mikkelsen — and this is exactly where it came back.
09bbf46a3deb: <t1>1825—1878</t1> <t2><t3>Thomas Jensen</t3> — smallholder, fisherman and beach bailiff at Økjær. Lost at sea on 9 November 1878; the first of the family to be written down with the name Silkjær — in the deed of 1876.</t2>
21b96fad026e: <t1>1855—1928</t1> <t2><t3>Niels Thomsen Silkjær</t3> — smallholder, fisherman and boatman in the lifeboat service. The man who made Silkjær a fixed, hereditary family name.</t2>
235f569955dd: <t1>1883—1956</t1> <t2><t3>Ane Johanne</t3> — one of his ten children. Married the master mason Mads Erik Madsen of Rækker Mølle; the first of the line to leave the coast altogether.</t2>
